channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: You Get One-Third Less at Tullamarine
item.description: A comparison of the newly opened Tullamarine Airport with Sydney's Kingsford Smith finds Melbourne's terminal consistently one-third smaller in every measure, from baggage carousels and immigration desks to souvenir koalas and VIP lounges.

item.title: What's Mr. Playboy Doing in a Dedman Suit?
item.description: Playboy's men's fashion director Robert L. Green visits Melbourne to show how the magazine covers male style, but arrives wearing a dull grey Dedman suit and a wide paisley tie, confirming that Australian fashion lags three years behind New York.

item.title: Batman at Botany Bay Where It Looked as if Cook Discovered a Used-Car Yard
item.description: Keith Dunstan travels to Sydney for the Captain Cook bicentenary celebrations, finding Kurnell choked with cars and plastic pennants, a re-enactment hampered by failed electronics, and the Aboriginal community at La Perouse watching the festivities with a complicated grief.

item.title: All Boys in the Ban, But for a Naughty Neighbor
item.description: Victoria's struggle to maintain public decency is undermined at every turn by South Australia, where Don Dunstan allows 'Portnoy's Complaint' to be sold, wears shorts to Parliament and presides over the longest drinking hours in Australia, prompting Keith Dunstan to quote at length a Victorian preacher's Victorian-era pamphlet on the perils of self-pollution.

item.title: A Time When Ladies Can Become Gentlemen
item.description: The 1970 VFL Grand Final, won by Carlton, is examined through the flood of newspaper supplements, the record-breaking crowd of 121,696, scalpers charging up to $60 a seat, and the curious instance of men removing their make-up to gain admission through the MCG's ladies' reserve.

item.title: Will Little Audrey Skip on for Ever?
item.description: The return of the Skipping Girl Vinegar sign to Abbotsford, celebrated by Barry Humphries in verse, prompts a wider survey of the National Trust's classification system and a plea to extend it under 'Batman's Law' to the State Theatre, Flinders Street Station, the Exhibition Building fountain, and even the small iron pissoir at Flinders and Exhibition Streets.

item.title: One Ray of Sunshine Threatens a Reputation
item.description: A week of unusually withering comment about Melbourne, from a visiting Clement Freud who called it an ideal city for escaping Dartmoor, to Robin Boyd lamenting the loss of creative spirit in its architecture, and Barry Humphries delivering a fond but cutting ode to its musical-comedy qualities, prompts Keith Dunstan to wonder whether becoming internationally understood will cost Melbourne its carefully nourished reputation.

item.title: Flashpoints on the Bunyip's Intimate Parts
item.description: A private screening of John Murray's censored documentary film 'The Naked Bunyip' at the Palais Theatre, with the censored passages flagged by coloured lamps, reveals the contradictions of Australian film censorship in 1970, from pack rape to Barry Humphries, prostitutes and a toothpaste commercial.

item.title: That Was the Year That Was 1970
item.description: A satirical prediction column for Melbourne in 1970, forecasting the Tullamarine Airport opening, Sir Henry Bolte's election strategy, a disappointing VFL season, the "Hair" and "Oh! Calcutta!" controversies, the mining boom, the fashion industry's maxi-skirt battle, and the general human comedy of city life.

item.title: This Game's Nearly as Bad as Aussie Rules
item.description: A dispatch from the Melbourne Stock Exchange gallery during the Poseidon mining boom, comparing the feverish broking-floor atmosphere to barracking at the MCG, and gently mocking the euphemistic language finance writers reach for when the market gets nervous.

item.title: Skipping Around a Rewarding Tragedy
item.description: A review of D. L. Bernstein's social history of the Melbourne Cup, "First Tuesday in November," tracing the race from its origins under Captain Standish through the legends of Archer, Poseidon and Jimmy Ah Poon, and celebrating the Cup's role in Australian national life.

item.title: The Night I Was Kept Awake by a Belly Dancer
item.description: A TV nightmare about automated television broadcasting leads into a genuine account of surviving an HSV-7 movie marathon from midnight to 8 a.m., taking in Humphrey Bogart, Mel Ferrer's possessed strangling hands, Modigliani's death scene, and the redeeming glory of Laurel and Hardy in "The Blockheads."

item.title: Just the Shot for Mad Dogs and Englishmen
item.description: A war-correspondent account of joining the opening day of the duck shooting season in the Riverina near Hay, where 100-plus camouflaged gunmen mobilise before dawn through swamp mud, with pre-battle keg, army-surplus logistics, and a dog so faithful it kept retrieving the one protected water hen someone shot by mistake.

item.title: If You've Got Wine, Who Needs Women and Song?
item.description: A report on the Rutherglen Wine Festival, which drew 20,000 visitors to a town of 1600, featuring free wine at the wineries, a street procession with a working still on the back of a truck, a barrel-rolling contest, hay-bale singing under the stars, and the election of a Vintage Queen from candidates including Miss Riesling, Miss Port and Miss Claret.

item.title: There's Something to Be Said for the Old John Bull
item.description: As Melbourne prepares for the 1970 royal tour, Keith examines a surprising royalist revival led by Brigadier Richard Eason's British Brotherhood, which seeks one flag, one anthem and a common Commonwealth defence, while Myer stages a British week complete with a Santa Claus dressed as John Bull.

item.title: A Man with Real Power Behind His Attack
item.description: A profile of William O. Bourke, managing director of Ford Motor Company of Australia, who has launched a public campaign blaming politicians rather than car makers for Australia's road toll, and who proposes a 10-point plan including better roads, tougher licensing, real punitive measures for drunk drivers, and the abolition of trams.

item.title: What a Beautiful Baby Is Leading the Pre-Poll Parade
item.description: In the weeks before the Victorian state election, a rush of government announcements, from the South Eastern Freeway extension to new trains and a tower hotel beside the Regent Theatre, illustrates how the pre-poll season resembles football's heady opening round of optimism.

item.title: Now Is the Time for All Good Men to Come to the Aid of Their Trousers
item.description: Melbourne's male-only pub culture crumbles as the new Eureka Stockade tavern throws open all its bars to women, tracing a long history from colonial mateship and female shortages through to the last bastions at Flemington's Members Stand and the Melbourne Club.

item.title: A Night in the Clink for the National Trust
item.description: The National Trust throws a champagne party inside the condemned Melbourne Gaol, as rival plans for Pentridge Prison and proposals for a $40 million redevelopment leave Melbourne's most magnificently horrible jails facing uncertain futures.

item.title: I'm in the Moog for Love
item.description: Melbourne jingle-maker Bruce Clarke demonstrates his newly acquired $12,000 Moog synthesiser, the electronic marvel capable of creating any sound on earth, from Arctic blizzards to canaries singing Twinkle Twinkle Little Star with an elastic band accompaniment.

item.title: See What Happens When Rules Become a Religion
item.description: The opening of the VFL football season reveals a new industrial mood among players, with strikes at Collingwood and Essendon over pay, prompting speculation about a Footballers' Association of Victoria aligned with the ACTU.

item.title: When Is a Floor Not a Floor? When It's a Living Experience
item.description: Two new exhibitions at Melbourne galleries, an undulating timber floor built from Whelan the Wrecker salvage at Gallery A in South Yarra and a Philip Morris air-themed show at the National Gallery, test Keith Dunstan's willingness to take conceptual art seriously.

item.title: Boys Will Be Boys — or Is It a Girl?
item.description: A Geelong court case in which a young man assaulted someone he took to be a boy prompts a field guide to identifying the sexes in the age of unisex fashion, covering make-up, hair, footwear, trousers and handbags, with a final tip borrowed from James Laver that the creature acting like the boss is almost certainly female.

item.title: Ho, Yo-Yo and a Bottle of Coke
item.description: A Coca-Cola sponsored yo-yo promotion at the Southern Cross Hotel gives Keith Dunstan occasion to mourn the passing of spontaneous childhood hobbies, from hula hoops and go-carts to silkworms and cigarette cards.

item.title: Once Upon a Time — or Things Could Be Better
item.description: A rueful reckoning with Melbourne's reputation, prompted by Opposition leader Clyde Holding calling the city 'the little Chicago' after a run of murders, armed hold-ups and kidnappings, set against the city's traditional pride in its Sunday decorum and its virtuous contrast with Sydney.

item.title: Bendigo's Magic Dragon Gives Its Last Puff
item.description: The centenary of Bendigo's Easter Fair Parade brings two dragons into the streets, Old Loong making his final public appearance after nearly a century, and a magnificent new 200-foot dragon, Sun Loong, arriving from Hong Kong to take his place.

item.title: The Way to Make a Million in Australiana
item.description: Melbourne goes mad for Australiana-themed restaurants and bars, with the Hotel Australia's Wool Shed, the Commodore Motel's Eureka Stockade complex, and the Branding Iron all opening within weeks of each other, leading Keith Dunstan to announce his own Instant Australiana Mart.

item.title: Taxes That Take the Fun Out of Life
item.description: The federal budget's new wine tax prompts an elegy for the great Melbourne tradition of home bottling, with Dan Murphy lamenting the death blow to a joyous, laughing industry, while Keith Dunstan proposes compensating taxes on yoghurt, rosehips and Coca-Cola to make the wowsers pay their share.

item.title: Oh, for the Return of the Eminent Dr. Clutterbuck
item.description: The decision to demolish the Regent Theatre and replace it with a 53-storey hotel and office tower signals the end of the Paris End of Collins Street, as the accelerating destruction of the city's nineteenth-century buildings proceeds from the Coates ice-cube tray to the Oriental Hotel.

item.title: Down in the Depths About Going Up in the Air
item.description: A world tour of airports, culminating at Boeing's vast Everett factory outside Seattle, finds the jumbo jet age transforming air travel into an exhausting exercise in walking while making the aircraft themselves look like ocean liners coming in to berth.
